Design: the wire format and the redundancy math

Source: vignettes/design.Rmd
design.Rmd
library(csvschema)

A CSV passed between programs is a one-way broadcast over an erasure channel: rows vanish, cells get damaged, and there is no way to ask the sender for a resend. The internet solved the same problem decades ago by assuming a hostile channel and encoding everything else. csvschema borrows three of its ideas: fragmentation metadata, per-piece integrity, and whole-object verification.

A packet is one ASCII token

Every piece of the schema is a single unquoted token of the form {{<id>~<payload>~<crc>}}. No comma, semicolon, tab, pipe, quote, newline, or whitespace appears inside it, so no CSV dialect ever needs to quote it and no delimiter rewriting can change it. Non-ASCII bytes are percent-encoded and spaces become +:

cs_encode_token("Public charity")
#> [1] "Public+charity"
cs_encode_token("Café")
#> [1] "Caf%C3%A9"

Here are the actual packets for a small schema:

s <- cs_schema(
  data.frame(ein = "001234567", year = 2020L, rev = 1.5,
             org = factor("Public charity"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  primary_key = "ein",
  overrides = list(ein = list(constraints = list(pattern = "^[0-9]{9}$",
                                                 unique = TRUE)))
)
writeLines(cs_packetize(s, mtu = 200))
#> {{S0/6~cs=1^enc=utf-8^dialect=rfc4180^fields=4^rows=1^mtu=200^hash=5a946b1530b8~231d3cf8}}
#> {{S1/6~ein^str^pat=%5E%5B0-9%5D%7B9%7D%24^uniq~935ecb9f}}
#> {{S2/6~year^int~e127d914}}
#> {{S3/6~rev^num~86934540}}
#> {{S4/6~org^str^lev=Public+charity~694de026}}
#> {{S5/6~pk=ein~111401d0}}

Packet S0 is the header (wire version, encoding, dialect, field count, row count, MTU, and the whole-schema hash). Packets S1..Sn are the fields in column order, and the last schema packet carries table-level properties such as the primary key. Each packet’s attribute keys map one-to-one onto Frictionless Table Schema v2 field properties, so the sidecar and the packets are two encodings of the same model.

Three internet ideas, translated

Internet mechanism Purpose csvschema analogue
IP identification group fragments of one datagram schema hash in packet 0
IP fragment offset position of this piece k in S/
IP more-fragments flag know when all pieces are in P carried in every packet
TCP/UDP checksum, Ethernet CRC discard damaged pieces CRC-32 suffix per packet
BitTorrent info-hash reject mixed versions whole-schema hash recomputed after reassembly
TCP retransmission recover loss via back-channel not available; repetition coding instead
PAR2 / fountain codes recover loss with no back-channel repetition now; erasure type reserved
Path MTU max piece the link accepts mtu argument

Each packet carries its own index and the total count, rather than a last-piece flag, because a flag fails when the last piece is the one lost. Each packet ends with a CRC-32 over id~payload; a packet that fails is dropped as if its row had been deleted. After reassembly, the whole-schema hash in packet 0 is recomputed — so a plausible mix of two schema versions is rejected even though every individual packet is valid.

rec <- cs_recover(cs_parse_packets(cs_packetize(s)))
rec$status
#> [1] "verified"

How much redundancy?

Repetition coding makes survival a coupon-collector problem. If a fraction f of rows is kept at random and each packet has r independent copies, a union bound over P packets gives the minimum copies as ceiling( ln(P / eps) / -ln(1 - f) ), which cs_copies() computes:

f <- c(0.50, 0.20, 0.10, 0.05, 0.01)
data.frame(
  retained = f,
  copies   = vapply(f, function(fi) cs_copies(20, fi, eps = 1e-6), integer(1))
)
#>   retained copies
#> 1     0.50     25
#> 2     0.20     76
#> 3     0.10    160
#> 4     0.05    328
#> 5     0.01   1673

cs_redundancy() turns a required r into a concrete layout — a number of schema columns c and packets per cell p — preferring extra packets per cell (invisible) over extra columns, and cs_survival() reports the achieved failure probability for any layout:

cs_redundancy(20, 2000, f = 0.2)$sentence
#> [1] "survives random loss of 80% of rows with failure probability 4.1e-09"
cs_survival(20, 2000, c = 1, p = 1, f = 0.2)
#> [1] 4.074072e-09

Striping

Random row loss is the easy case. Structured loss — a head(), a page of a paginated export, a systematic every-k-th sample — is handled by a deterministic rotating stripe, so the packets are spread rather than clustered. cs_stripe() is pure arithmetic, so it is reproducible and testable:

cs_stripe(P = 4, N = 8, c = 1, p = 1)
#>      [,1]
#> [1,] 0   
#> [2,] 1   
#> [3,] 2   
#> [4,] 3   
#> [5,] 1   
#> [6,] 2   
#> [7,] 3   
#> [8,] 0

The stripe guarantees that the first P rows contain every packet (so a head() recovers), that any 2P - 1 consecutive rows do, that a full read does, and that the systematic every-P-th-row sample cycles through all packets. A single period-P stripe cannot also guarantee every arbitrary strided sample in its first P terms — that is mathematically incompatible with the contiguous guarantee — so heavy arbitrary strides rely on the redundancy r, not on the stripe.

What the format cannot do

Three limits are worth stating plainly:

  • Deleting every _schema column removes the in-band schema entirely. Use the sidecar (cs_write(..., sidecar = TRUE)), which is independent, or accept that the file reads back as character columns with status = "absent".
  • Case-folding every cell is detected, not recovered: the per-packet CRC covers the exact-case payload, so folded payloads fail and are dropped.
  • NA versus "": with the default missingValues = [""], an empty cell reads back as NA; the two are indistinguishable once written with na = "". Numeric values are written at R’s default precision.

Erasure coding (which would recover from fewer surviving rows but destroy human readability and add a dependency) is reserved for a future version; the E packet type is left unused for it.
